title: Meredith Fraser
text: I am from Halifax, Nova Scotia. I have a Bachelor of Science in Marine Biology and a Master’s in Resource Management. I have a keen interest in marine and ocean sciences, and I am an advocate for evidence-based environmental conservation. Prior to MDS I researched seagrass ecology on the Atlantic Coast of NS and worked in marine plant management on both the Pacific and Atlantic Coasts of Canada. I am currently completing the Master’s of Data Science (MDS) program at the University of British Columbia. In the MDS program I am building my knowledge and applied skills in programming and modelling to utilize data to answer community-driven research questions in the fields of marine and environmental sciences.

title: My first weeks in MDS
text:
First couple of weeks on campus.


The MDS program kicked off in the last week of August, 2026 with a whirlwind three days of orientation events. During orientation, I had the chance to meet my fellow classmates, professors, and all the folks who help keep the program running, as well as get acquainted with the program structure and the UBC West Point Grey campus.
Having spent very little time on the UBC campus prior to starting the program, I was surprised by just how big campus is (read: accepting any and all insight on shortcuts for commuting between classes in the 10 min breaks) and also by how much green space there is on campus. Having access to the Pacific Spirit Regional Park has been a gift and I anticipate going on many trail runs in the park over the next 10 months while I complete the MDS program.
While I did manage to get lost on several occasions on campus in these first few weeks and I suspect it may be a few more weeks before git add/commit/push become as second nature to me as breathing is, I would like to think I am otherwise finding my feet in the MDS program and my new home in Vancouver. The courses are engaging, the materials interesting, our professors and TAs are helpful and supportive, and I am looking forward to what comes next.

title: Visualizing the palmer penguins data Python
text:
In this blog, we are going to examine the palmer penguins dataset (Gorman et al., 2014; Palmer Penguins Dataset, 2014) using python. Data were collected and made available by Dr. Kristen Gorman and the Palmer Station, Antarctica LTER.
I am interested in finding out which island (recorded from 3 islands in the Palmer Archipelage, Antarctica) has the longest average flipper length (cm) for all the Adelie penguin species measured (only species with flipper length measurements from all 3 islands).
I will first start by organizing or ‘tidying’ the data for our question.

# Import the required libraries
import pandas as pd
from palmerpenguins import load_penguins

# Load the penguins dataset
penguins = load_penguins()

# Clean up the dataset and prep for summarizing and visualizing
## Drop `NaNs` from the flipper_length_mm column (the variable we are interested in) 
penguins_clean = penguins.dropna(subset=['flipper_length_mm'])
## Create a new column: flipper_length_cm (converting mm to cm)
penguins_clean['flipper_length_cm'] = penguins_clean['flipper_length_mm']/100
## Filter for only the Adelie penguin species, and select only the required columns for our question (island, flipper_length_cm)
penguins_clean = penguins_clean.query("species == 'Adelie'").loc[:,['island','flipper_length_cm']]

# Print the head of the tidy penguins dataset
print(penguins_clean.head())

      island  flipper_length_cm
0  Torgersen               1.81
1  Torgersen               1.86
2  Torgersen               1.95
4  Torgersen               1.93
5  Torgersen               1.90


Now we can group the tidied data by island, to calculate the mean flipper length in cm, and then sort the resulting means from longest to shortest.

penguins_summary = (
    penguins_clean
    .groupby(['island'])['flipper_length_cm']
    .mean()
    .sort_values(ascending=False)
    .reset_index()
)

I want to produce a clean-looking table with the three islands sorted according to longest flipper length (measured in cm) for the Adelie penguin species.

Adelie_flipper_table = penguins_summary.style.hide(axis="index")
Adelie_flipper_table






island
flipper_length_cm




Torgersen
1.911961


Dream
1.897321


Biscoe
1.887955





As you can see in the table, the average flipper length (cm) for all Adelie penguin species is very similar across the three islands sampled, however Adelie penguins on Torgersen had the longest flipper length on average.
References
Gorman, K. B., Williams, T. D., & Fraser, W. R. (2014). Ecological sexual dimorphism and environmental variability within a community of Antarctic penguins (genus Pygoscelis). PloS one, 9(3), e90081. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0090081
Palmer Penguins [Dataset]. (2014). UCI Machine Learning Repository. https://doi.org/10.24432/C5R89W

title: Visualizing the palmer penguins data with R
text:
In this blog, we are going to examine the palmer penguins dataset (Gorman et al., 2014; Palmer Penguins Dataset, 2014) using R. Data were collected and made available by Dr. Kristen Gorman and the Palmer Station, Antarctica LTER.
I am interested in visualizing which island (recorded from 3 islands in the Palmer Archipelage, Antarctica) has the longest average flipper length (cm) for all the Adelie penguin species measured (only species with flipper length measurements from all 3 islands).
I will first start by organizing or ‘tidying’ the data for our question.

library(tidyverse)
library(palmerpenguins)

# Clean up the dataset and prep for summarizing and visualizing
penguins_clean <- penguins |>
    ## Drop `NAs` from the flipper_length_mm column (the variable we are interested in) 
    drop_na(flipper_length_mm) |>
    ## Create a new column: flipper_length_cm (converting mm to cm)
    mutate(flipper_length_cm = flipper_length_mm/100) |>
    ## Filter for only the Adelie species and select only the required columns for our question (island, flipper_length_cm)
    filter(species == "Adelie") |>
    select(island, flipper_length_cm)

# Print the head of the tidy penguins dataset
head(penguins_clean)

# A tibble: 6 × 2
  island    flipper_length_cm
  <fct>                 <dbl>
1 Torgersen              1.81
2 Torgersen              1.86
3 Torgersen              1.95
4 Torgersen              1.93
5 Torgersen              1.9 
6 Torgersen              1.81


Now we can group the tidied data by island, to calculate the mean flipper length in cm for all Adelie penguins measured on that island.

penguins_summary <- penguins_clean |>
    group_by(island) |>
    summarise(mean_flipper_length_cm = mean(flipper_length_cm)) 

I want to produce a bar plot of average flipper length (cm), by island for the Adelie penguin species.

ggplot(data = penguins_summary, mapping = aes(x = island, 
                                      y = mean_flipper_length_cm,
                                     fill = island)) +
    geom_col(size = 2) +
    xlab("Penguin Species") +
    ylab("Flipper length (cm)") +
    theme_bw() +
    theme(text = element_text(size = 18))

Warning in geom_col(size = 2): Ignoring unknown parameters: `size`








Figure 1





As you can see in Figure 1, the average flipper length (cm) for all Adelie penguin species is very similar across the three islands sampled, however Adelie penguins on Torgersen had the longest flipper length on average.
References
Gorman, K. B., Williams, T. D., & Fraser, W. R. (2014). Ecological sexual dimorphism and environmental variability within a community of Antarctic penguins (genus Pygoscelis). PloS one, 9(3), e90081. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0090081
Palmer Penguins [Dataset]. (2014). UCI Machine Learning Repository. https://doi.org/10.24432/C5R89W

title: About
text: I have a keen interest in marine and ocean sciences, and I am an advocate for evidence-based and community-led environmental stewardship. I have over four years of professional experience in both scientific research and applied resource management roles with a focus on marine plant biology and ecology. Over the last three years in my role as an Aquatic Science Biologist with Fisheries and Oceans Canada, I have conducted several experiments to measure the climate-driven responses of eelgrass, a coastal foundation species that provides fish habitat, protects our shorelines, and sequesters blue carbon.
